source_read: PDF PDFs/Cocaine/Barnett_1981_CocainePKHumans.pdf, pp. 353–366, final published version (scanned pages with a machine-read text layer that misreads some numbers; all 14 pages read on images rendered at 150 dpi, Tables 2 and 3 and Fig. 5 also at 300 dpi; every number used checked on the rendered page)

claims.overstatement: None for the parts taken from this source; the claim reports the half-lives, the five-session basis of the dose equations, the calibration problem and the second-hand nature of the intranasal figures accurately. One simplification: 'the level then halved every 79 to 82 minutes after 200 mg' describes the terminal phase only; in both 200 mg sessions the first hour fell faster or irregularly (W's curve needed a two-exponential fit with an early-phase half-life of 13.0 minutes, p. 363; Z fell from 2530 to 963 ng/ml between 5 and 15 minutes and then levelled at about 1000 ng/ml to 60 minutes, Table 1, p. 357). 'Terminal half-life' or 'in the later hours' would be exact.
claims.note: Every number from this source in the statement and magnitude was found on the printed page: 4 men; 100 or 200 mg infused over about 1.5 to 3 minutes; at least 48 hours without cocaine; first (5-minute) samples 921, 682 and 1005 ng/ml after 100 mg (range 682 to 1005) and 3868 and 2530 ng/ml after 200 mg, the highest in each session; terminal half-lives 51.5, 40.3 and 47.2 minutes after 100 mg and 82.3 and 78.9 after 200 mg (51.5 against 82.3 in W); intranasal F 0.6 and absorption half-life 8.4 minutes from a refit of Javaid et al. (1978b) mean curves sampled to 1.5 hours; five sessions behind the dose equations; standard curves 2 to 500 ng/ml. The machine-read text gives 41.2 for Y's half-life; the printed Table 3 shows 47.2, and 0.693/β from Table 2 gives 47.1 (my calculation; the other four reproduce as 51.3, 40.3, 82.3 and 78.8). 'Early values lie above the assay's calibrated range' is a reader's inference, not the authors' statement, and it is correct: every 5-minute value and most first-hour values after 200 mg exceed 500 ng/ml. 'Gave doses in an order that was not randomized': no randomization, placebo or blinding is described, and the order of W's two sessions is not stated (Z's 200 mg session preceded his repeated-dose session). Two omissions the editor may weigh. (1) The sentence 'None of the studies read tested what happens when people take more because they feel little at first' is literally true, but this paper reports one repeated-dose session: Z received a second 100 mg 30 minutes after the first, and 5 minutes later his level was 6990 ng/ml, about five times the 1374 ng/ml predicted by adding the first dose's 5- and 30-minute values (my calculation; the authors say 400% above), which they read as possible accumulation (p. 363; Fig. 5, p. 362). It is one session in one man, not in the Methods, and the value lies far above the calibrated range, so it could only be reported as a single observation with those limits, and as a finding, never as guidance. (2) For snorting, the paper's 8.4-minute figure rests on an absorption rate constant with a 72% coefficient of variation (Table 2, p. 358), the authors say sparse samples around the peak prevented a better estimate (p. 361), they report the observed peak in those averaged data as between 20 and 60 minutes (p. 361), and their second intranasal dataset (topical application, Van Dyke et al., 1978) gave 20.4 minutes and a relative F of about 0.3, a comparison they call questionable (Table 3, p. 360; p. 361). 'Poorly estimated' would be a fair addition. No sentence drawn from this source reads as advice on amounts or routes; the doses appear as study conditions.

anchors.locator: Methods › Clinical protocol, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (the 3rd continuing on p. 355); Methods › Chemical analysis, 3rd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Four male volunteers with documented frequent cocaine self-administration over the preceding 6 months, at doses the authors call comparable to the study's; at least 48 h without cocaine before each session. Three received 100 mg; one of them and one further man received 200 mg in a separate session (five sessions). Cocaine in 1.5 ml infused intravenously over about 1.5 to 3 min; 10 ml blood samples from the other arm every 5 to 60 min over 3 to 6 h. Standard curves spanned 2 to 500 ng/ml of plasma.

anchors.locator: Results and discussion › Intravenous data, 1st paragraph; Table 1
anchors.extracted: The first sample, drawn 5 min after the injection, was the maximum in every session: 921 (W, 68 kg), 682 (X, 95 kg) and 1005 ng/ml (Y, 58 kg) after 100 mg; 3868 (W) and 2530 ng/ml (Z, 86 kg) after 200 mg. At 60 min: 430, 170 and 477 ng/ml after 100 mg, 1222 and 990 after 200 mg; at 120 min after 100 mg: 190, 88 and 199 ng/ml. Text: about 700 to 1000 ng/ml at 5 min after 100 mg, falling to 200 to 500 at 1 h and 100 to 200 at 2 h. Every 5-minute value exceeds the 500 ng/ml top of the standard curve (p. 354).

anchors.locator: Table 3, column t1/2(β); Table 2 (p. 358), column β
anchors.extracted: Terminal half-lives 51.5 (W), 40.3 (X) and 47.2 min (Y) after 100 mg; 82.3 (W) and 78.9 min (Z) after 200 mg. Recomputed as 0.693/β from Table 2: 51.3, 40.3, 47.1, 82.3 and 78.8 min (my calculation). W's 200 mg curve was the only two-exponential fit (α 0.0532 per min, coefficient of variation 43%); its early-phase half-life is given as 13.0 min (p. 363).

anchors.locator: Results and discussion › Dose dependence, 1st paragraph (p. 361, continuing to p. 363); Figs 2 and 3 (p. 362)
anchors.extracted: Half-life regressed on dose over 1.05 to 2.94 mg/kg: t1/2 = 13.5 + 24.5 × dose, r = 0.946; clearance = 2.51 − 0.67 × dose, r = −0.973; volume of distribution r = −0.89. The authors state the dose dependence rests on only five sets of data, with W's two sessions the only within-person comparison (dose 1.47 to 2.95 mg/kg: half-life +60%, volume −28%, clearance −55%). No P values or intervals.

anchors.locator: Review of literature, 3rd paragraph (p. 356); Literature data, 1st paragraph and Table 2 (p. 358); Pharmacokinetic parameters, 1st paragraph (p. 359), 4th paragraph (pp. 360–361) and 5th paragraph (p. 361); Table 3 (p. 360)
anchors.extracted: Intranasal figures come from refitting the published mean curves of Javaid et al. (1978b): 10 volunteers given 32 mg intravenously and 96 mg by nasal inhalation, assayed without an internal standard (only the high doses used). Intranasal absorption half-life 8.4 min, its rate constant poorly estimated (coefficient of variation 72%); F = 0.6, 'based on averaged plasma data'; sampling only to 1.5 h, so peak time and terminal half-life are called poor estimates; observed peak between 20 and 60 min; sparse points near the peak prevented a better estimate. A second intranasal dataset (topical application, Van Dyke et al., 1978, n = 4) gave 20.4 min and a relative F of about 0.3, called questionable.

anchors.locator: Results and discussion › Dose dependence, 2nd paragraph; Fig. 5 (p. 362)
anchors.extracted: One repeated-dose session, not in the Methods: Z received 100 mg and a second 100 mg 30 min later; the level 5 min after the second dose was 6990 ng/ml against a predicted 820 + 554 ng/ml, which the authors call 400% above prediction (about five times, my calculation), suggesting possible accumulation; terminal half-life 94.9 min against 78.9 after his single 200 mg dose. One session in one man; the value lies far above the calibrated range.
The authors call their findings tentative: the intravenous studies had few participants and the literature analyses rest on averaged data.

key_findings.correction: Values, weights and per-kg doses (1.47, 1.05, 1.72, 2.94, 2.33 mg/kg) checked on the rendered Table 1; the two rises in the decline (W 352 then 430; X 254 then 290) are as stated.
47.2 for Y confirmed on the rendered page; 0.693/0.0147 = 47.1.
Editors' calculation reproduced: 13.4 + 24.5 × dose, r = 0.945; clearance r = −0.973; volume (L/kg) r = −0.890; Fisher-z interval for r = 0.946 with n = 5: 0.385 to 0.997.
Reported as the authors state it. A + B = 2482 + 1997 = 4479 ng/ml; the linear prediction at 2.94 mg/kg is about 1895 ng/ml, so 4479 is about 136% above (the authors' 140%).
6990/1374 = 5.1. Fig. 5 checked at 300 dpi: triangles match Z's 200 mg values in Table 1; the circles show about 7000 ng/ml at 35 minutes and about 6000 at about 40 minutes.

Editors' calculation reproduced: 55.7% of the intranasal AUC lies beyond 90 minutes; F recomputes as 0.58. Precision: the authors' 'not good estimates' because of sampling to 1.5 hours concerns peak time and terminal half-life (p. 359); for the absorption half-life they cite large coefficients of variation and sparse points near the peak (pp. 360–361).

reporting_issues.note: Calibration 2–500 ng/ml (p. 354) against 5-minute values of 682–3868 ng/ml (Table 1) and 6990 ng/ml (p. 363).
Zeros: X at 240, 300 and 360 minutes; Y at 360 minutes (Table 1).
Oral α: text 7%, Table 2 20%; intranasal topical: text 34–61%, Table 2 34–68%.
Per-kg 5-minute values recomputed: 626, 648, 583, 1088 (Z) and 1315 (W) ng/ml per mg/kg.

risk_of_bias.note: Overall high agreed: the dose comparison is mostly between people, with no randomization, placebo or tests, and early values exceed the calibrated range. The terminal half-lives themselves rest mostly on later samples within the calibrated range, so they are less affected than clearance, AUC and initial concentrations.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial: the Summary presents five-session equations as general results and states intranasal bioavailability and absorption rates that are refits of another laboratory's averaged data.

missed: Observed peak time in the refitted intranasal (Javaid et al., 1978b) mean data: between 20 and 60 minutes (p. 361, Pharmacokinetic parameters, 4th paragraph). It is the only intranasal peak-time statement in the paper and bears on the snorting comparison in cl_coc_pk_route.

The authors' statement that the exponential fit underestimates the initial concentration at 2.9 mg/kg by 33% (p. 362) does not reproduce from the printed equation: 185 × e^2.94 ≈ 3499 ng/ml against A + B = 4479 ng/ml, about 22% (my calculation). Minor.

Barnett et al. estimated the lower limit of reliability of the Javaid et al. assay at 50–100 ng/ml and used only that study's high-dose data for this reason (p. 356); the card records only the missing internal standard.
